newsitem.title: CANADA: Magnesium industry must be competitive - Ford.
newsitem.headline: Magnesium industry must be competitive - Ford.

text.p: The magnesium industry should take the initiative, and quickly, to develop new products in the auto industry in the face of strong competition from polymers and aluminum, Gerald Cole of Ford Motor Co told delegates at the World Magnesium Conference.
"We don't have any magnesium organizations who are proactive today in design and production," Cole said, referring to diecast auto components, the light metal's biggest growth sector.
Magnesium usage in auto parts has risen from 9,000 tonnes in 1984 to about 60,000 tonnes on an annual basis currently. The global magnesium market is about 300,000 tonnes.

Over the next decade the magnesium market is expected to grow from 300,000 tonnes to 500,000 tonnes, all due to diecasting parts for autos, Cole said. "We need a strategic understanding of what our industry is to do," Cole said.
Ford is the world's biggest user of engineered magnesium products, consuming some 15,000 tonnes annually.

Cole also suggested that the International Magnesium Association, a U.S. based industry organization which organized the Toronto meeting, should widen its membership from just producers, to include consumers and manufacturers of products.

At the conference a representative from Toyota Motor Co in Japan said growth of diecast components in the Asian market will be restricted because magnesium was too expensive. The price would have to equal aluminum to be competitive.
Magnesium is twice as expensive as aluminum.

Cole told Reuters later it was unrealistic to expect that magnesium prices would fall to the same level as aluminum, but a ratio of magnesium prices at 1.8 times those of aluminum should be the maximum. Today's price ratio was "untenable", Cole said.

The Big Three U.S. auto makers, and U.S. Department of Energy are part of a Partnership for New Generation of Vehicles (PNGV), a quest to develop a 6-passenger mid-sized vehicle with a goal of three liter/100 km fuel efficiency by 2004.

As part of this plan, the PNGV met last week to hammer out a "magnesium roadmap" - a 5-year plan which would require $31.7 million funding to boost magnesium consumption in cars. A boost in magnesium consumption in auto manufacturing is considered necessary as the light metal helps reduce weight.

Cole said the "roadmap" included a list of issues which magnesium needed to tackle, including better manufacturing, more rapid tooling, methods of recycling the metal and cheaper metal. Technical challenges also lay ahead.
Cole said funding for the roadmap had not yet been agreed.

Ford has already agreed to pump nearly A$40 million into a pilot magnesium smelter in Queensland State, Australia which, if successful, will be expanded to a 90,0000 tonnes commercial plant at a cost of A$700 million.
Ford has no plans to invest in the commercial smelter but would take up half the output for ten years.

The Big Three could not agree to develop one car to meet the PNGV goals, and each was pursuing its own project. Ford is currently developing its P2000 car with a more aggressive fuel efficiency goal and reducing total mass of the car by 30 percent or 450 kilograms.
The P2000 is scheduled to contain 39 kilograms of magnesium, a sharp hike on the 4.5 kilograms in today's Ford Taurus model, Cole said.
Two years ago, however, Ford forecast it would use 100 kg in each car by 2005, but since then some components were found unobtainable in the metal, Cole said.
